title: On Bits and Atoms (#2)
body_html:
My last writing was about how the “Bits vs Atoms” debate ignores that bits are instantiated physically and tend to interact with other physical objects (see: self-driving cars, robotics, GPS, and rockets).

What else is missing from this frame? People.

To be fair, the debate points to one part of the world of people (government, more on this later) as a reason for the gap between progress in the world of bits and that of atoms. But both by emphasis and breadth, the importance of the social layer tends to be underweighted in these conversations.

Of course, just like computers, humans belong to the world of atoms. But to take this debate literally would be mistaken. Atoms, in the sense intended by Negroponte and Thiel, are what engineers arrange to create non-digital products and experiences. Bits are infinitely reproducible abstractions stored in computers and observable through screens. Let’s create a trichotomy, with humans as the consumers, governments, producers, financiers, entrepreneurs, and, more broadly, the entire social context these bits and atoms exist within.

In the same way something in the world of bits may be constrained by the world of atoms (e.g., an AI system’s training run being limited by power or compute) or vice versa (hardware lacking intelligence), both of these worlds may be constrained by the world of humans.

The set of things belonging to the world of humans is large, difficult to define, and likely overlapping. Here are some categories of note:

Government (western, democratic context): a superstructure that imperfectly balances the will of its people against a set of agreed-upon principles. It shapes incentives through taxation and regulation, creates and enforces laws, and directs resources toward market failures. Governments may fail - due to an influential and mistaken constituency, bureaucracy, self-dealing, or any number of causes - to allow for the conditions that would permit an otherwise transformative and productive technology or product to create change.

Consumers: the set of individuals and organizations that buy products and services, and therefore produce signals for producers of products and services to act upon. Consumers may fail to adopt a product or service due to behavioral frictions, superstition, a lack of awareness, or any number of other reasons, despite the product being “better” in some abstract sense.

Capital: Like consumers, capital allocators make decisions about where to invest resources (money, expertise, marketing, industry connections) into businesses. Capital may, and does, overvalue businesses or sectors, while under-investing in others. Capital is largely directed by humans, who tend to crowd into narratives. This creates volatile, reflexive markets, somewhat detached from the underlying economic activity (and products) they are meant to fund and price. Especially in the short run.

The above categories are incomplete. The point is that the social context any given technology or product - no matter which “world” it belongs to - exists within will be massively influential on its success. There are narrow, specific determinants of a product’s success, like a government’s anti-trust laws or tax policy, but also broader ones, like the social histories of a population.
